# Agent instructions: glasses-free 3D web pages with @displayxr/inline3d

For any coding agent (OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Claude Code without the plugin, others). Copy this file
into a project as `AGENTS.md` (or point your agent at it) when the project builds pages on
[`@displayxr/inline3d`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@displayxr/inline3d).

## How to call the tools

The tools are the npm package `@displayxr/inline3d-tools`, pinned to an exact version. **In a
sandboxed agent, prefer the MCP server** (below): MCP servers run outside the sandbox, while a shell
`check` starts a local file server and headless Chrome, which OpenAI Codex's default sandbox blocks
(`listen EPERM 127.0.0.1`), so there it needs the user to approve running the command outside the
sandbox. Otherwise run them as shell commands:

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 check <url | dir | page.html> [--root <project>] [--max-texture 4096]
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets <file.glb> [--target tablet|desktop]
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets prep <in> <out.glb> [--metres 0.01] [--decimate 0.5]
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 scaffold <esm|vite> <target-dir> --title "<page title>"
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 gen providers | gen run <adapter> ... --confirm-paid | gen provenance --file ...
```

or, with the MCP server configured (`inline3d-tools mcp`; config snippets for Codex, Cursor and
Claude Code in this package's README), call its tools with the same
semantics: `check`, `asset_check`, `scaffold`, `gen_providers`, `gen_run` (paid: pass
`confirm_paid: true` only after the user approved that one call and its cost),
`gen_provenance`, `authoring_guide` (returns this file). Relative paths resolve against the
server's working directory.

Needs Node ≥ 18; `check` also needs a local Chrome or Chromium (`CHROME=/path/to/chrome`).
Generator keys come only from the environment (`MESHY_API_KEY`, `TRIPO_API_KEY`,
`OPENAI_API_KEY`); never ask for, print, log or write one.

## Building on @displayxr/inline3d

A woven window is a `<canvas>` whose **buffer holds two eyes side by side** while its CSS box is the
shape the viewer sees. The DisplayXR Browser weaves it; every other browser shows the page in 2D.
The installed package is the source of truth: read `node_modules/@displayxr/inline3d/llms.txt` first,
then the docs below **from `node_modules/@displayxr/inline3d/`** (they match the installed version;
this file does not copy them). The `.d.ts` files there carry the full API with JSDoc.

### 1. Pick the content type and entry point

| You have | Call | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| a side-by-side 3D photo | `wall.addImage(canvas, 'pic_2x1.jpg')` | SDK sizes the buffer; style only the box |
| an SBS 3D video element | `wall.addVideo(canvas, videoEl)` | VP9/WebM plays everywhere; `.mp4` may not |
| a video with transport UI | `addPlayer(wall, canvas, src, opts)` from `/player` | canvas must sit in a container; `format: 'mono'` for 2D titles |
| a glTF/GLB model | `addModel(wall, canvas, url, opts)` from `/model` | PlayCanvas by default; `engine: 'three'` for three.js; Draco/KTX2 decoders are files YOU serve |
| a Gaussian splat (.sog/.ply) | `addSplat(wall, canvas, src, { engine: 'playcanvas' })` from `/splat/playcanvas` | the page behind the tile shows around the splat (§4: keep it soft, or pass an opaque `clearColor`); Spark (three) is the `/splat` default; PlayCanvas adds `setSource`, effects, streaming |
| your own three.js / WebGL scene | `wall.addScene(canvas, onFrame, opts)` + `EyeCamera` from `/three` | you render each eye into `layer.getViewport(view)` |

`addModel` / `addSplat` / `addPlayer` take the wall and work with an unsupported one (they draw the
2D fallback themselves). Prefer them over a hand-written scene whenever the content fits: they size
the buffer, clamp it to the device, frame the subject on the glass, and validate frames.
three or PlayCanvas: use PlayCanvas for models and splats (the default, the most tested path); use
three when the page already is a three.js app (`addScene` + `EyeCamera`, see
`docs/porting-three-js-apps.md`).

### 2. Pick the rig by what the user moves

- The user turns a **subject** (model, product, diorama, chart, avatar), even with an orbit control:
  **display rig** (the default). Keep an existing orbit camera and pose the portal from it:
  `displayRig({ position: target, orientation: camera.quaternion, virtualDisplayHeight: 2*d*tan(fov/2) })`.
- The user moves **through a world** (first person, game, map, walkthrough, ported VR): **camera rig**,
  `cameraRigFromCamera(THREE, cam, { convergence })`, set per frame with `handle.setViewRig`.
  A game is a world even when it is seen from above (an RTS, a board, a top-down map the user pans
  and zooms): the camera moves, so it is a camera rig. Tie `convergence` to the ground at the view
  centre (raycast the centre of the screen to the ground plane), not to the cursor or a gaze point,
  and cap zoom-in so the comfort product stays ≤ 1.
- Details: `docs/authoring-inline-3d.md` § View rigs. Comfort on a camera rig:
  `ipdFactor × metersToVirtual × convergenceDiopters × ~0.6` must stay ≤ 1; never `convergence: 0`.

### 3. Depth and comfort (`docs/making-3d-look-right.md`, nine rules)

Centre the subject on z = 0 (the glass), at real proportions; don't push it back or flatten it.
`+z` is OUT of the glass. Frame the whole subject in the first view. Tilt flat layouts 25–40° about an
axis through the glass. Keep moving things' forward swing small. Worlds: fixed convergence, keep the
camera clear of near geometry. Light/mid-tone low-contrast backgrounds (never pure black behind a
bright subject). Text as HTML near the glass, not in the scene. No coplanar faces (z-fighting), no
sub-pixel detail. Scene units: metres for a `virtualDisplayHeight` (0.24 by default); never scale the
world per frame. Shrinking depth: rotate or scale uniformly, never squash z.

### 4. Woven-canvas checklist (`docs/woven-canvas-rules.md`)

- [ ] **One** `createInline3D()` per document (or `sharedInline3D()`); `close()` on `pagehide`.
- [ ] **One persistent canvas**; never remount it on state change (React keys, Strict Mode). Swap
      content inside it (`setSource`, redraw the source, change the scene). `add*()` twice on a canvas
      is not a swap: `remove()` first.
- [ ] **No CSS effects on the canvas or any ancestor**: `filter`, `opacity < 1`, `mask`, `clip-path`,
      `mix-blend-mode`, `backdrop-filter`, scale/rotate transforms. No `border`, `border-radius`,
      `box-shadow` on the canvas (use `cornerRadius` / `feather`). Never animate the tile's box.
- [ ] **Cover a new canvas** with an opaque element on top until `await handle.firstWoven`, then remove
      it with a hard cut, and ALSO on a timeout (~4 s) and in `catch`, so it always comes off. A
      `firstWoven` with `woven: false` still means "drop the cover and keep drawing both eyes".
      **Video and players too:** `loadeddata`, `canplay`, a player's `'ready'` and the first decoded
      frame all fire BEFORE the join, so a cover released there shows the raw pair for up to ~1.2 s.
      Release on `handle.firstWoven` (`addVideo`), `player.firstWoven` (`addPlayer`, SDK 1.53+; on an
      older SDK where it is undefined, wait for the first frame and then `firstWovenHoldMs` ≈ 1200 ms
      more), plus the timeout. Give a player a `poster`: it is painted into both eyes under the cover.
- [ ] **What is behind a transparent tile is part of the picture.** `addSplat` / `addModel` clear
      transparent by default, and the browser pre-blends the page under both eyes, flat, at half
      horizontal resolution. Make that page area a soft light or mid-tone colour or gradient (no
      text or photo behind a tile, never black behind a bright subject), or pass an opaque
      `clearColor: [r, g, b, 1]` (0..1).
- [ ] **`onLayerLost` goes flat** (`addScene` pages): pass `onLayerLost` and, in it, render ONE mono
      camera across the whole canvas on your own rAF loop (the `!wall.supported` path) or show a 2D
      fallback. An empty `() => {}` leaves the last side-by-side pair on screen, unwoven. `SceneViewer`:
      `onLayerLost: viewer.onLayerLost`; `addSplat` / `addModel` / `addPlayer` handle it themselves.
- [ ] **Nothing opaque above the canvas**; backgrounds and black go *under* it. Never overlap two
      woven canvases (hide the lower one with `display: none`).
- [ ] **Buffer = 2 × eye width**: `addScene` pages size it themselves (2× the box aspect, devicePixelRatio
      ≤ 2, every side ≤ 4096 for tablets) and draw into `gl.drawingBufferWidth/Height`. three.js:
      `renderer.setPixelRatio(1)` when you use `getViewport()`.
- [ ] **Validate before you clear**: skip the clear when `views.length < 2` or a viewport is `null`;
      repaint the last good frame. Copy `XRViewport` / `XRView` fields by name (their fields are
      getters: spread and `Object.assign` copy nothing). Redraw every frame.
- [ ] **Never draw one full-width flat picture into a woven canvas.** To show 2D on purpose, call
      `wall.setStereoEnabled(false)` (fall back to easing `ipdFactor` to 0 on `NotSupportedError`).
- [ ] **2D fallback**: on `!wall.supported` render one mono view or show an `<img>` (the left eye),
      never the packed side-by-side pair. `createInline3D()` can also **reject**. Guard it with
      `await createInline3D().catch(() => null)` (or `try`/`catch`) and treat `null` like
      `!wall.supported`. An uncaught rejection leaves the page with no 3D and no 2D fallback.

### 5. Page chrome, HUD and detection

- Detect by capability: `await createInline3D()` → `wall.supported`, or `inline3DAvailable()` as a sync
  pre-gate. **Never** the user-agent string, never `navigator.xr.isSessionSupported('inline-3d')`.
- Current browsers occlude woven tiles with 2D by draw order: a sticky header the tile scrolls
  under, a buy card in a corner, badges, menus and captions over a tile just work, **opaque or
  translucent**, as plain HTML (a solid or rgba background and text). Keep them **partial** (a bar,
  a card, a pill): a section painted over the WHOLE tile hides it while it keeps rendering.
- What does NOT work over a tile: a pixel-moving `filter` (blur, drop-shadow), a `mix-blend-mode`
  other than normal, `transform-style: preserve-3d` on the chrome; the tile weaves through them.
  `backdrop-filter` (frost) is fine on DisplayXR Browser 0.1.16+ over a **partial** region (the tile
  is drawn flat under it), never over a whole visible tile. If you must also serve older browsers,
  use a near-solid `rgba(…, .92)` bar without blur.
- Hide chrome with `display: none`, not `opacity: 0`. Ask `inline3dOcclusionByDrawOrder()` only to
  drop legacy calls. The checker scrolls the page and reports chrome that passes over a tile.
- HUD text and values: HTML beside or over the tile, readable size, not drawn into the 3D scene.

### 6. Pins (exact versions, no `^`)

`@displayxr/inline3d` **1.52.3**, `playcanvas` **2.24.0** (exact; `>=2.22.3 <3` is the supported
range), `three` **0.180.0**. CDN import maps pin the same: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@displayxr/inline3d@1.52.3/js/inline3d.js`,
`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/playcanvas@2.24.0/build/playcanvas.mjs`,
`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.180.0/build/three.module.js`. If a newer SDK is installed, its
`CHANGELOG.md` says what changed; prefer the installed version's docs over this list.

### 7. Before you say done: run the checker

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 check <url | dir | page.html> [--root <project>] [--max-texture 4096]
```

This runs the exact-pinned `@displayxr/inline3d-tools` package from npm (the first run downloads it;
the user may be asked to approve the command). Needs Node ≥ 18 and a local Chrome (`CHROME=/path/to/chrome`).
If the `inline3d-tools` MCP server is configured, its `check` tool is the same check (and the route
to use inside a sandbox that blocks local servers).
It loads the page in headless Chrome inside a fake DisplayXR Browser (two real eye views) and again
plain, and reports pass/fail per check: session reached, real stereo, no blank eye, no flat
side-by-side, buffer not clamped, CSS/cover/overlay/session rules (scrolling the page past each
tile), the page going flat when the session ends (`onLayerLost`), console and GL errors, 2D
fallback, plus the rig, comfort and measured depth. Fix every **FAIL**; read every **WARN**; each
line names the doc section. For a Vite/dev-server app pass the running URL. Use `--root <project>`
when a page imports `../` or `/node_modules/`. A green run is not a panel test: say so, and ask for
a check on real hardware when depth or look matters. Scaffold a known-good page with the "Scaffold an inline-3D page" section below. Any model, texture or poster the page loads goes through the "Assets for inline-3D pages" section below first (convert, optimise, `assets` check, `ASSETS.md`).

**When to run it.** After you edit any file of a page that uses `@displayxr/inline3d` (its HTML,
scripts or CSS), the page is unchecked until the checker has run again: run it before you tell the
user the page is done, and again after every round of fixes. If you end a turn with an edited page
you could not check (no Chrome, no Node, the user declined the command), say so in one line and give
the user the command above to run.

## Scaffold an inline-3D page

The templates ship in the exact-pinned `@displayxr/inline3d-tools` npm package; its `scaffold`
command copies them (the first run downloads the package; the user may be asked to approve the command):

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 scaffold esm  <target-dir> --title "<page title>"
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 scaffold vite <target-dir> --title "<page title>" [--name <npm-name>]
```

It never overwrites an existing file (`--force` replaces). What it writes:

| file | what |
|---|---|
| `app.js` | the page logic (shared by both flavours): a three.js scene on `addScene` with `EyeCamera`, display rig, validate-before-clear with last-good replay, buffer sized 2× the box (dpr ≤ 2, clamped to the GPU), cover removed on `handle.firstWoven` + a 4 s timeout + `catch`, a mono 2D fallback |
| `style.css` | page styles; the canvas and its ancestors carry no CSS effects |
| `index.html` (esm) | no build step: an import map with exact CDN pins |
| `index.html` + `package.json` (vite) | Vite: exact npm pins (`@displayxr/inline3d` 1.52.3, `three` 0.180.0) |

### Steps

1. Pick the flavour: **esm** unless the project already uses npm/a bundler (then **vite**, or merge
   the pins into the existing `package.json` exactly, no `^`).
2. Run `scaffold` with the flavour and the target directory (it fills in the title and, for vite,
   the package name). Don't add an `<img>` or extra canvas: there is ONE persistent canvas.
3. Pick the content (the "Building on @displayxr/inline3d" §1 table) and swap the scene block if it is not a custom
   scene. Keep the cover, the fallback and the pins. For a model or a splat, replace everything from
   "renderer + scene" down with the viewer call, which handles the buffer, framing, validation and
   the 2D fallback itself:

   ```js
   import { createInline3D } from '@displayxr/inline3d';
   import { addModel } from '@displayxr/inline3d/model';          // or: import { addSplat } from '@displayxr/inline3d/splat/playcanvas';
   const wall = await createInline3D().catch(() => null);           // unsupported -> the viewer draws 2D
   const handle = addModel(wall, canvas, './assets/model.glb');     // addSplat(wall, canvas, './scene.sog', { engine: 'playcanvas' })
   // the page behind the tile shows around the subject: keep it a soft colour (or pass clearColor)
   Promise.race([handle.firstWoven, new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 4000))]).finally(dropCover);
   ```

   A player is the same shape: `addPlayer(wall, canvas, ['./clip.webm', './clip.mp4'], { poster })`
   from `/player` (webm first; the canvas sits in a container for the transport), and the cover
   comes off on `player.firstWoven` + the timeout, never on `'ready'` / `loadeddata`. On an SDK
   without `player.firstWoven`, wait for the first frame and then ~1200 ms more.

   Add `"playcanvas": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/playcanvas@2.24.0/build/playcanvas.mjs"` and
   `"@displayxr/inline3d/model": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@displayxr/inline3d@1.52.3/js/inline3d-model-entry.js"`
   (or `.../js/inline3d-splat-pc-entry.js` for `/splat/playcanvas`) to the import map, or
   `"playcanvas": "2.24.0"` to `package.json`. Images and video use `wall.addImage(canvas, 'pic_2x1.jpg')`
   / `wall.addVideo(canvas, videoEl)` in the 3D branch and an `<img>` of the left half (or a mono
   video) in the 2D branch. Check each export against the installed `.d.ts` before using it.
4. Run it: esm → serve the directory (`python3 -m http.server`), or let the checker
   serve it; vite → `npm install && npm run dev`.
5. **Run the checker before saying done**, and fix every FAIL:

   ```sh
   npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 check <target-dir>              # esm
   npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 check http://localhost:5173/    # vite dev server
   ```

The untouched template passes every check (verdict PASS). If your change makes a check fail, the
failing line names the rule and the doc in `node_modules/@displayxr/inline3d/docs/`.

## Assets for inline-3D pages

Both eyes draw every triangle and sample every texture, the weakest device is a tablet with a
4096 px texture limit, and depth errors that a 2D page hides (sorting, z-fighting, a model that is
centimetres instead of metres) show in stereo. So every asset goes through the same three steps:
**get it → prepare it → check it**, and every asset gets a line in `ASSETS.md`.

Tools, in the order to reach for them:

| Tool | When | Install |
|---|---|---|
| `inline3d-tools assets` | always, last | `npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets` (exact pin, from npm; Node only) |
| glTF-Transform CLI | glTF/GLB in, glTF/GLB out: inspect, resize, compress, simplify, centre | `npx -y @gltf-transform/cli@4.3.0` (pinned; nothing installed globally) |
| Blender (headless) | any other format (FBX, OBJ, STL, PLY, DAE, .blend), units/axis fixes, heavy decimation | **only if already installed**; never install it |
| `inline3d-tools gen` | no asset exists and the user wants one generated | `npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 gen`; needs the user's own API key in the environment; every call is paid and needs the user's yes |

### 1. Get it

In order of preference:

1. **The user's own asset** (in the project, or a path they gave). Record it:
   `npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 gen provenance --file assets/x.glb --source "supplied by the user" --license "user's"`.
2. **A library asset with a clear licence** (CC0 / CC-BY, e.g. the Khronos glTF sample models,
   Poly Haven). Record the URL, author and licence; CC-BY needs visible credit on the page.
3. **A placeholder you build** (primitives in three.js/PlayCanvas) when nothing fits and the user
   did not ask for generation. Say so in your notes.
4. **Generation**, only when the user asked for it or agreed. See §4.

Never take a model from a site whose licence you cannot state.

### 2. Prepare it

**glTF/GLB (glTF-Transform).** Look first, then fix only what the check flags:

```sh
GT="npx -y @gltf-transform/cli@4.3.0"
$GT inspect in.glb                                   # triangles, textures, extensions, size
$GT optimize in.glb out.glb --compress false --texture-compress webp --texture-size 2048
```

That default (WebP textures resized to 2048, deduplicated, pruned, no geometry compression) needs
**no decoder** on the page. Only for big meshes add `--compress meshopt` and then the
`meshoptimizer` package (an import-map entry or `package.json` pin): nothing to serve. Avoid
`--compress draco` and KTX2 unless the page already serves `/draco/` and `/basis/` (the SDK never
fetches decoders from a CDN). Other fixes: `$GT simplify in.glb out.glb --ratio 0.5 --error 0.001`
(too many triangles), `$GT center in.glb out.glb --pivot center` (the origin is far from the model),
`$GT copy in.gltf out.glb` (a multi-file .gltf → one file you cannot half-deploy).

**Anything else (Blender, if present).** Detect it, don't install it:

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets prep in.fbx out.glb [--metres 0.01] [--decimate 0.5] [--blender <path>]
```

It looks for Blender (`--blender`, `$BLENDER`, `PATH`, the default install location), never installs
it, and runs the package's headless prep script, which imports, applies transforms, scales to
metres (`--metres` = metres per source unit: 0.01 for centimetres), decimates, recentres the bounds on the origin and exports one GLB. Then run
the glTF-Transform `optimize` line on its output (Blender writes PNG textures; WebP is far smaller).
No Blender: say the format cannot be converted here, and ask for a GLB.

Units: `addModel` frames the model on the glass from its bounds, so units and offset do not break
it; a model you place in your own `addScene` must be in **metres, centred** (its real size: a
helmet is ~0.3 m, not 2 m).

### 3. Check it (before the page uses it)

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets out.glb            # tablet budget (default)
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 assets out.glb --target desktop
```

It reports: missing external files, decoders the page must provide, triangles (both eyes draw
them; tablet budget 300k), draw calls, size/units/pivot, texture sizes and decoded GPU memory
(over 4096 px fails on a tablet), alpha-BLEND materials (sorting errors read as depth errors in
stereo; use MASK for cut-outs), metallic/glass materials (they need an environment map: keep
`addModel`'s default image-based environment (`'room'` / `'neutral'`) or pass `envMap`; never
`environment: 'studio'`, a punctual rig under which metal renders dark), file size, and
animations. Fix every FAIL; act on WARNs or say why not. Then run the page checker ("Building on @displayxr/inline3d" §7): the asset check is about the file, the page check about how it is shown.

### 4. Generate it (optional, paid, the user's keys)

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 gen providers     # which adapters have a key (names only)
```

Adapters: `meshy` and `tripo` (text-to-3d, image-to-3d → GLB), `openai` (image → PNG, for
textures, posters and backdrops). Each reads its key from the environment (`MESHY_API_KEY`,
`TRIPO_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`) and from nowhere else.

**Rules, no exceptions:**
- **Never ask for, print, echo, log, write or commit a key.** Never put one in a file, an env file
  you create, a command line, or `ASSETS.md`. If no key is set, the adapter is unavailable: say so
  and use §1 instead. Do not suggest pasting a key into the chat.
- **Ask before every paid call.** Tell the user the adapter, what you will generate (the prompt or
  image), and the cost estimate `gen run` prints; only after they say yes run it with
  `--confirm-paid`. Without that flag `gen run` refuses and prints the estimate. One yes covers
  one call, not a batch, unless the user said otherwise.
- **Every generated file goes through §2 and §3** (generated models are often huge, off-centre,
  with 4K textures), and `gen run` has already written its `ASSETS.md` line (adapter, prompt,
  date, the provider's licence note). Check the provider's licence terms before calling the asset
  shippable.

```sh
npx -y @displayxr/inline3d-tools@0.1.0 gen run meshy --kind text-to-3d --prompt "a brass desk lamp, PBR" --out assets/lamp-raw.glb --confirm-paid
```

### 5. ASSETS.md

One table, at the project root, one row per file the page loads that you did not write: file,
source (URL, "supplied by the user", or `generated: <adapter> <kind>`), licence, date, notes
(prompt, author, changes made: "optimised: webp 2048, decimated 50%"). Create it with the
`provenance` command; keep it in the deliverable. A CC-BY asset also needs a visible credit on the
page.
